On the motive of the Quot scheme of finite quotients
of a locally free sheaf

Andrea T. Ricolfi Address: SISSA, Via Bonomea 265 Trieste Email address, Andrea T. Ricolfi : atricolfi@gmail.com
Abstract.

Let XX be a smooth variety, EE a locally free sheaf on XX. We express the generating function of the motives [QuotX⁡(E,n)][\Quot_{X}(E,n)] in terms of the power structure on the Grothendieck ring of varieties. This extends a recent result of Bagnarol, Fantechi and Perroni for curves, and a result of Gusein-Zade, Luengo and Melle-Hernández for Hilbert schemes. We compute this generating function for curves and we express the relative motive [QuotAd(𝒪⊕r)→SymAd][\Quot_{\mdmathbb A^{d}}(\mathscr{O}^{\oplus r})\rightarrow\Sym\mdmathbb A^{d}] as a plethystic exponential.

Key words and phrases:
Quot schemes, Moduli spaces of sheaves, Grothendieck ring of varieties.

0. Introduction

Let XX be a smooth quasi-projective variety over C\mdmathbb C, and let EE be a locally free sheaf of rank rr on XX. The Quot scheme QuotX⁡(E,n)\Quot_{X}(E,n) parameterises quotients EQE\twoheadrightarrow Q such that QQ is a zero-dimensional sheaf of length nn. Recently Bagnarol, Fantechi and Perroni [1] have shown that if CC is a smooth proper curve, the class

[QuotC⁡(E,n)]∈K0​(VarC)\bigl[\Quot_{C}(E,n)\bigr]\,\in\,K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{\mdmathbb C})

in the Grothendieck ring of varieties does not depend on EE. We use the theory of power structures [8] to extend their result to arbitrary dimension. Roughly speaking, a power structure on a ring RR is a way of making sense of expressions A​(t)mA(t)^{m}, where A⁡(t)=1+A1​t+A2​t2+⋯A(t)=1+A_{1}t+A_{2}t^{2}+\cdots is a power series with coefficients in RR and m∈Rm\in R.

For (X,E)(X,E) as above, we form the generating function

𝖹E​(t)=∑n≥0[QuotX⁡(E,n)]​tn,\mathsf{Z}_{E}(t)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\,\bigl[\Quot_{X}(E,n)\bigr]t^{n},

and we denote by 𝖯r,n∈K0​(VarC)\mathsf{P}_{r,n}\in K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{\mdmathbb C}) the motive of the punctual Quot scheme, namely the closed subscheme Pr,n⊂QuotX⁡(E,n)P_{r,n}\subset\Quot_{X}(E,n) parameterising quotients that are entirely supported at a single (fixed) point in XX.

Our first main result (proved in Theorem 2.3) is the following.

Theorem A.

There is an identity

𝖹E​(t)=(∑n≥0𝖯r,n​tn)[X].\mathsf{Z}_{E}(t)=\left(\sum_{n\geq 0}\mathsf{P}_{r,n}t^{n}\right)^{[X]}.

Since the punctual Quot scheme only depends on rr, nn and dimX\dim X, it follows that the same holds true for the motive of QuotX⁡(E,n)\Quot_{X}(E,n). Note that this was proved for r=1r=1 (the Hilbert scheme case) by Gusein-Zade, Luengo and Melle-Hernández [9].

Our second main result is of relative nature and concerns X=AdX=\mdmathbb A^{d}. The Quot-to-Chow morphism

QuotX⁡(E,n)→Symn⁡X\Quot_{X}(E,n)\rightarrow\Sym^{n}X

sends a quotient EQE\twoheadrightarrow Q to the support of QQ, viewed as a zero-cycle with multiplicities. We consider the relative motive

𝖹rel(Ad,r)=∑n≥0[QuotAd(𝒪⊕r,n)→SymnAd]∈K0(VarSym⁡Ad)\mathsf{Z}^{\rel}(\mdmathbb A^{d},r)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\,\bigl[\Quot_{\mdmathbb A^{d}}(\mathscr{O}^{\oplus r},n)\rightarrow\Sym^{n}\mdmathbb A^{d}\bigr]\,\in\,K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{\Sym\mdmathbb A^{d}})

over the symmetric product of Ad\mdmathbb A^{d}. We define classes ∈r,nK0(VarC){}_{r,n}\in K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{\mdmathbb C}) by

∑n≥0𝖯r,n​tn=Exp⁡(∑n>0tnr,n)\sum_{n\geq 0}\mathsf{P}_{r,n}t^{n}=\Exp\left(\sum_{n>0}{}_{r,n}t^{n}\right)

where Exp\Exp is the motivic exponential (see Section 1.5) induced by the lambda ring structure on K0​(VarC)K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{\mdmathbb C}). For Ad\mdmathbb A^{d}, we refine Theorem A by showing (see Theorem 2.9) that 𝖹rel​(Ad,r)\mathsf{Z}^{\rel}(\mdmathbb A^{d},r) is generated on the small diagonal by the absolute motives r,n.

Theorem B.

There is an identity

𝖹rel(Ad,r)=Exp∪(∑n>0r,n[Ad→�nSymnAd]).\mathsf{Z}^{\rel}(\mdmathbb A^{d},r)=\Exp_{\cup}\left(\sum_{n>0}{}_{r,n}\boxtimes\bigl[\mdmathbb A^{d}\xrightarrow{\Delta_{n}}\Sym^{n}\mdmathbb A^{d}\bigr]\right).

See [6, 13] for analogues of this result in the context of motivic Donaldson–Thomas theory and [3] for the calculation of the (absolute) virtual motive of Hilbn⁡(A3)\Hilb^{n}(\mdmathbb A^{3}).

Finally, our last result (see Section 3.1) is the full “solution” of the motivic theory of the Quot scheme of a smooth curve, which can be summarised by the identities

r,n={[Pr−1]if ​n=10if ​n>1.{}_{r,n}=\begin{cases}[\mdmathbb P^{r-1}]&\textrm{if }n=1\\ 0&\textrm{if }n>1.\end{cases}
Theorem C.

If EE is a locally free sheaf on a smooth curve CC, there is an identity

𝖹E​(t)=Exp⁡([C×Pr−1]​t).\mathsf{Z}_{E}(t)=\Exp\left(\bigl[C\times\mdmathbb P^{r-1}\bigr]t\right).

Moreover, in K0​(VarSym⁡A1)K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{\Sym\mdmathbb A^{1}}) there is an identity

𝖹rel(A1,r)=Exp∪([Pr−1][A1→idA1]).\mathsf{Z}^{\rel}(\mdmathbb A^{1},r)=\Exp_{\cup}\left(\bigl[\mdmathbb P^{r-1}\bigr]\boxtimes\bigl[\mdmathbb A^{1}\xrightarrow{\id}\mdmathbb A^{1}\bigr]\right).

We use the first relation to compute the Hodge–Deligne polynomial of the smooth space QuotC⁡(E,n)\Quot_{C}(E,n) for a proper curve CC (Proposition 3.5). We stress that the formula for 𝖹E\mathsf{Z}_{E} in the proper case was already implicit in the calculation of [1, Prop. 4.5].

In Section 3.3 we discuss the case r=1r=1 on a surface, where we find 1,n=Ln−1{}_{1,n}=\mdmathbb{L}^{n-1} according to Göttsche’s formula [7]. Finally, we conclude by proposing a geometric open problem related to punctual Quot schemes on curves.

We work over the field of complex numbers throughout.

1. Motivic preliminaries

In this section we recall a few motivic constructions that will be needed later. Most of this material is a simplified version of [6, Section 1], adapted to suit the purposes of this paper.

1.1. The Grothendieck ring of varieties

Fix a complex scheme SS locally of finite type over C\mdmathbb C. The Grothendieck ring of SS-varieties

K0​(VarS)K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{S})

is the free abelian group generated by isomorphism classes [X→S][X\rightarrow S] of SS-varieties modulo the scissor relations, namely the identities

[X→𝑓S]=[Y→f|YS]+[X∖Y→f|X∖YS]\bigl[X\xrightarrow{f}S\bigr]\,=\,\bigl[Y\xrightarrow{f|_{Y}}S\bigr]+\bigl[X\setminus Y\xrightarrow{f|_{X\setminus Y}}S\bigr]

imposed whenever Y⊂XY\subset X is a closed SS-subvariety of XX. The ring structure is given on generators by fibre product over SS,

(1.1) [X→S]⋅[Y→S]=[X×SY→S].[X\rightarrow S]\cdot[Y\rightarrow S]=[X\times_{S}Y\rightarrow S].

The element

L=[A1×CS→S]∈K0(VarS)\mdmathbb{L}=[\mdmathbb A^{1}\times_{\mdmathbb C}S\rightarrow S]\,\in\,K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{S})

is called the Lefschetz motive (over SS). If S′S^{\prime} is another complex scheme, there is an external product

(1.2) K0​(VarS)×K0​(VarS′)→K0​(VarS×S′)K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{S})\times K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{S^{\prime}})\xrightarrow{\boxtimes}K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{S\times S^{\prime}})

defined on generators by sending ([f:X→S],[g:X′→S′])↦[f×g:X×X′→S×S′]([f\colon X\rightarrow S],[g\colon X^{\prime}\rightarrow S^{\prime}])\mapsto[f\times g\colon X\times X^{\prime}\rightarrow S\times S^{\prime}].

A morphism f:S→Tf\colon S\rightarrow T induces a ring homomorphism f∗:K0​(VarT)→K0​(VarS)f^{\ast}\colon K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{T})\rightarrow K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{S}) by base change and a K0​(VarT)K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{T})-linear map f!:K0(VarS)→K0(VarT)f_{!}\colon K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{S})\rightarrow K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{T}) defined on generators by composition with ff.

Definition 1.1.

We denote by S0​(VarS)S_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{S}) the semigroup of effective motives, i.e. the semigroup generated by isomorphism classes [X→S][X\rightarrow S] of complex quasi-projective SS-varieties modulo the scissor relations. The product (1.1) turns S0​(VarS)S_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{S}) into a semiring. There is a natural semiring map S0​(VarS)→K0​(VarS)S_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{S})\rightarrow K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{S}), and we say that �∈K0​(VarS)\alpha\in K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{S}) is effective if it lies in the image of this map.

1.2. Equivariant motives and the quotient map

Recall that if SS is a scheme with a good action by a finite group GG (i.e. an action such that every point of SS has an affine GG-invariant open neighborhood), the quotient S/GS/G exists as a scheme. For instance, finite group actions on quasi-projective varieties are good.

Definition 1.2.

Let GG be a finite group, SS a scheme with good GG-action. We denote by K~0G​(VarS)\widetilde{K}_{0}^{G}(\mathrm{Var}_{S}) the free abelian group generated by isomorphism classes [X→S][X\rightarrow S] of GG-equivariant SS-varieties with good action, modulo the GG-equivariant scissor relations. We denote by K0G​(VarS)K_{0}^{G}(\mathrm{Var}_{S}) the quotient of K~0G​(VarS)\widetilde{K}_{0}^{G}(\mathrm{Var}_{S}) by the relations

[V→X→S]=[AXr],[V\rightarrow X\rightarrow S]=[\mdmathbb A^{r}_{X}],

where V→XV\rightarrow X is a GG-equivariant vector bundle of rank rr over a GG-equivariant SS-variety XX.

There is a natural ring structure on K~0G​(VarS)\widetilde{K}_{0}^{G}(\mathrm{Var}_{S}), where the product of two classes [X→S][X\rightarrow S] and [Y→S][Y\rightarrow S] is given by taking the diagonal action on X×SYX\times_{S}Y. The structures f∗f^{*}, f!f_{!} and \boxtimes naturally extend to the equivariant setting, along with their basic compatibilities. For instance, if f:S→Tf\colon S\rightarrow T (resp. g:S′→T′g\colon S^{\prime}\rightarrow T^{\prime}) is a GG-equivariant (resp. G′G^{\prime}-equivariant) map, and uu, vv are equivariant motives over SS, S′S^{\prime}, then

(1.3) (f×g)!(uv)=f!ug!v(f\times g)_{!}(u\boxtimes v)=f_{!}u\boxtimes g_{!}v

in the (G×G′)(G\times G^{\prime})-equivariant KK-group over T×T′T\times T^{\prime}.

One can define a K0​(VarS/G)K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{S/G})-linear map (cf. [6, Lemma 1.5])

(1.4) �G:K~0G​(VarS)→K0​(VarS/G)\pi_{G}\colon\widetilde{K}_{0}^{G}(\mathrm{Var}_{S})\rightarrow K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{S/G})

given on generators by taking the orbit space,

�G[X→S]=[X/G→S/G].\pi_{G}[X\rightarrow S]=[X/G\rightarrow S/G].

This map does not always extend to K0G​(VarS)K_{0}^{G}(\mathrm{Var}_{S}). It does when GG acts freely on SS, by [5, Lemma 3.2].

on effective classes A=[X→S]A=[X\rightarrow S], where �¯\overline{\nu} is the map Sn/𝔖n→SS^{n}/\mathfrak{S}_{n}\rightarrow S. One then uses the analogue of the relation (1.6) to find a unique set of lambda ring operators ��n\sigma_{\nu}^{n} restricting to the previous identity on effective motives.

As a special case, one can consider (S,�)=(N,+)(S,\nu)=(\mdmathbb N,+), viewed as a symmetric monoid in the category of schemes. We obtain lambda operations �n=�+n\sigma^{n}=\sigma^{n}_{+} on K0​(VarC)​⟦t⟧K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{\mdmathbb C})\llbracket t\rrbracket via the isomorphism

defined by sending ∑n≥0[Yn]tn↦[∐n∈NYn→{n}]\sum_{n\geq 0}[Y_{n}]t^{n}\mapsto\bigl[\coprod_{n\in\mdmathbb N}Y_{n}\rightarrow\set{n}\bigr].

1.4. Power structures

The main references for power structures are [8, 9].

Definition 1.3 ([8]).

A power structure on a (semi)ring RR is a map

(1+t​R​⟦t⟧)×R\displaystyle(1+tR\llbracket t\rrbracket)\times R →1+t​R​⟦t⟧\displaystyle\rightarrow 1+tR\llbracket t\rrbracket
(A⁡(t),m)\displaystyle(A(t),m) ↦A​(t)m\displaystyle\mapsto A(t)^{m}

satisfying the following conditions:

  1. (1)

    A​(t)0=1A(t)^{0}=1,

  2. (2)

    A​(t)1=A⁡(t)A(t)^{1}=A(t),

  3. (3)

    (A⁡(t)⋅B⁡(t))m=A​(t)m⋅B​(t)m(A(t)\cdot B(t))^{m}=A(t)^{m}\cdot B(t)^{m},

  4. (4)

    A​(t)m+m′=A​(t)m⋅A​(t)m′A(t)^{m+m^{\prime}}=A(t)^{m}\cdot A(t)^{m^{\prime}},

  5. (5)

    A​(t)m​m′=(A​(t)m)m′A(t)^{mm^{\prime}}=(A(t)^{m})^{m^{\prime}},

  6. (6)

    (1+t)m=1+m​t+O⁡(t2)(1+t)^{m}=1+mt+O(t^{2}),

  7. (7)

    A​(t)m|t→te=A​(te)mA(t)^{m}\big|_{t\rightarrow t^{e}}=A(t^{e})^{m}.

Throughout we use the following:

1.5. Motivic exponential

The motivic exponential is a group isomorphism

Exp:t​K0​(VarC)​⟦t⟧​→~​ 1+t​K0​(VarC)​⟦t⟧,\Exp\colon tK_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{\mdmathbb C})\llbracket t\rrbracket\,\widetilde{\rightarrow}\,1+tK_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{\mdmathbb C})\llbracket t\rrbracket,

converting sums into products and preserving effectiveness. If A=∑n>0An​tnA=\sum_{n>0}A_{n}t^{n} is an effective power series, one has by definition

Exp⁡(∑n>0An​tn)=∏n>0(1−tn)−An,\Exp\left(\sum_{n>0}A_{n}t^{n}\right)=\prod_{n>0}\,\bigl(1-t^{n}\bigr)^{-A_{n}},

and if AA and BB are effective, one sets

(1.9) Exp⁡(A−B)=∏n>0(1−tn)−An⋅(∏n>0(1−tn)−Bn)−1.\Exp(A-B)=\prod_{n>0}\,\bigl(1-t^{n}\bigr)^{-A_{n}}\cdot\left(\prod_{n>0}\,\bigl(1-t^{n}\bigr)^{-B_{n}}\right)^{-1}.

More generally, if (S,�:S×S→S)(S,\nu\colon S\times S\rightarrow S) is a commutative monoid in the category of schemes, with a submonoid S+⊂SS_{+}\subset S such that the induced map ∐n≥1S+×n→S\coprod_{n\geq 1}S_{+}^{\times n}\rightarrow S is of finite type, we similarly define

Exp�⁡(A)=∑n≥0��n​(A)\Exp_{\nu}(A)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\sigma_{\nu}^{n}(A)

on effective classes, and for AA and BB two effective classes, we define Exp�⁡(A−B)\Exp_{\nu}(A-B) by the analogue of (1.9), i.e. by Exp�⁡(A)⋅Exp�⁡(B)−1\Exp_{\nu}(A)\cdot\Exp_{\nu}(B)^{-1}.

1.6. Motives over symmetric products

The machinery described so far will be applied to the following situation. For a variety XX, we will consider (Sym⁡(X),∪)(\Sym(X),\cup), where

Sym⁡(X)×Sym⁡(X)→∪Sym⁡(X)\Sym(X)\times\Sym(X)\xrightarrow{\cup}\Sym(X)

In order to recover a formal power series in K0​(VarC)​⟦t⟧K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{\mdmathbb C})\llbracket t\rrbracket from a relative motive over Sym⁡(X)\Sym(X), we consider the operation

(1.10) #!(∑n≥0[Yn→SymnX])=∑n≥0[Yn]tn.\#_{!}\left(\sum_{n\geq 0}\,\bigl[Y_{n}\rightarrow\Sym^{n}X\bigr]\right)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\,[Y_{n}]t^{n}.

2.4. Related work on more general Quot schemes

The theory developed so far relies crucially on the locally free assumption on EE. Indeed, the isomorphisms (2.1) fail even if EE is, say, reflexive but not locally free. However, the geometry of the Quot scheme can be interesting also in the non-locally free case. For instance, the Quot scheme of finite quotients of the ideal sheaf ℐC⊂𝒪Y\mathscr{I}_{C}\subset\mathscr{O}_{Y} of a smooth curve in a 33-fold YY has been studied in [12], where essential local triviality statements on the Quot-to-Chow morphism were proved (see e.g. Corollary 3.2 in loc. cit.). Moreover, in [11, Thm. 2.1] it is proven that QuotY⁡(ℐC,n)\Quot_{Y}(\mathscr{I}_{C},n) appears as the typical (scheme-theoretic) fibre of the Hilbert–Chow morphism Hilb⁡(Y)→Chow⁡(Y)\Hilb(Y)\rightarrow\Chow(Y) in a neighborhood of the cycle of the smooth curve CC. (This holds in all dimensions, not just 33-folds.) This was used to prove the CC-local DT/PT correspondence for Calabi–Yau 33-folds [11, Thm. 1.1]. The (virtual) motivic theory of QuotY⁡(ℐC,n)\Quot_{Y}(\mathscr{I}_{C},n) was developed in [6].

The enumerative geometry of QuotX⁡(E,n)\Quot_{X}(E,n), for EE a sheaf of homological dimension at most one on a 33-fold, was studied in [2] and related to the local Pandharipande–Thomas theory of XX. The Appendix in loc. cit. develops the abstract theory comparing various Quot schemes of smooth quasi-projective varieties, and implicitly shows that the singularities of QuotX⁡(E,n)\Quot_{X}(E,n) only depend on nn and dimX\dim X. The (virtual) motivic theory in the locally free case for 33-folds was developed in [13], along with a construction of a virtual fundamental class on the Quot scheme.

(3.5) 𝖯r​(t)=Exp⁡([Pr−1]​t)=�Pr−1​(t)=∏i=0r−111−Li​t.\mathsf{P}_{r}(t)=\Exp([\mdmathbb P^{r-1}]t)=\zeta_{\mdmathbb P^{r-1}}(t)=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}\frac{1}{1-\mdmathbb{L}^{i}t}.

3.2. The Hodge numbers of the Quot scheme on a curve

The Hodge–Deligne polynomial (also called the E-polynomial) of a smooth complex projective variety YY is given by

𝖤⁡(Y,u,v)=∑p,q(−1)p+q​hp,q​(Y)​up​vq\mathsf{E}(Y;u,v)=\sum_{p,q}(-1)^{p+q}h^{p,q}(Y)u^{p}v^{q}

where hp,q(Y)=dimCHq(Y,)pYh^{p,q}(Y)=\dim_{\mdmathbb C}H^{q}(Y,{}_{Y}^{p}) are the Hodge numbers of YY. For instance, one has

(3.6) 𝖤⁡(Pr−1,u,v)=∑i=0r−1ui​vi,𝖤⁡(C,u,v)=1−g​u−g​v+u​v,\begin{split}\mathsf{E}(\mdmathbb P^{r-1};u,v)&=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}u^{i}v^{i},\\ \mathsf{E}(C;u,v)&=1-gu-gv+uv,\end{split}

where CC is a smooth projective curve of genus gg. Sending [Y]↦𝖤⁡(Y,u,v)[Y]\mapsto\mathsf{E}(Y;u,v) defines a motivic measure

K0​(VarC)→𝖤Z⁡[u,v]K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{\mdmathbb C})\xrightarrow{\mathsf{E}}\mdmathbb Z[u,v]

which is in fact a homomorphism of rings with power structure. The power structure on the polynomial ring Z⁡[u,v]\mdmathbb Z[u,v] is determined by the formula

(1−t)−f⁡(u,v)=∏i,j(1−ui​vj​t)−pi​j,(1-t)^{-f(u,v)}=\prod_{i,j}\,\bigl(1-u^{i}v^{j}t\bigr)^{-p_{ij}},

where we have written f⁡(u,v)=∑i,jpi​j​uj​vjf(u,v)=\sum_{i,j}p_{ij}u^{j}v^{j} for integers pi​jp_{ij}. This implies (cf. [9, Prop. 4]) the basic relation

(3.7) 𝖤⁡((1−t)−[Y])=(1−t)−𝖤⁡(Y,u,v).\mathsf{E}\left((1-t)^{-[Y]}\right)=(1-t)^{-\mathsf{E}(Y;u,v)}.

Let CC be a smooth projective curve of genus gg, and let EE be a rank rr locally free sheaf on CC. We compute the generating function

𝖤r​(C,t)=∑n≥0𝖤⁡(QuotC⁡(E,n),u,v)​tn.\mathsf{E}_{r}(C,t)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\mathsf{E}(\Quot_{C}(E,n);u,v)t^{n}.

We already know this series does not depend on EE.

Proposition 3.5.

There is an identity

(3.8) 𝖤r​(C,t)=∏i=0r−1(1−ui​vi+1​t)g​(1−ui+1​vi​t)g(1−ui​vi​t)​(1−ui+1​vi+1​t)\mathsf{E}_{r}(C,t)=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}\frac{(1-u^{i}v^{i+1}t)^{g}(1-u^{i+1}v^{i}t)^{g}}{(1-u^{i}v^{i}t)(1-u^{i+1}v^{i+1}t)}

in the ring Z⁡[u,v]​⟦t⟧\mdmathbb Z[u,v]\llbracket t\rrbracket.

Proof.

We have

𝖤r​(C,t)\displaystyle\mathsf{E}_{r}(C,t) =𝖤⁡(Exp⁡([C×Pr−1]​t))\displaystyle\,=\,\mathsf{E}\bigl(\Exp\bigl(\bigl[C\times\mdmathbb P^{r-1}\bigr]t\bigr)\bigr) by (3.1)
=𝖤⁡((1−t)−[C×Pr−1])\displaystyle\,=\,\mathsf{E}\left((1-t)^{-[C\times\mdmathbb P^{r-1}]}\right) by definition of Exp
=(1−t)−𝖤⁡([C×Pr−1])\displaystyle\,=\,(1-t)^{-\mathsf{E}([C\times\mdmathbb P^{r-1}])} by (3.7)
=(1−t)−(1−gu−gv+uv)∑i=0r−1uivi.\displaystyle\,=\,(1-t)^{-(1-gu-gv+uv)\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}u^{i}v^{i}}.

We have used that 𝖤\mathsf{E} is a ring homomorphism and the identities (3.6) in the last step. The result now follows from direct computation and by definition of the power structure on Z⁡[u,v]\mdmathbb Z[u,v]. ∎

Remark 3.6.

Setting u=vu=v in Formula (3.8) one recovers the generating function of (signed) Poincaré polynomials computed in [1, Remark 4.6], namely

∑n≥0P⁡(QuotC⁡(F,n),−u)​tn=∏i=0r−1(1−u2​i+1​t)2​g(1−u2​i​t)​(1−u2​i+2​t).\sum_{n\geq 0}P(\Quot_{C}(F,n),-u)t^{n}=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}\frac{(1-u^{2i+1}t)^{2g}}{(1-u^{2i}t)(1-u^{2i+2}t)}.

3.3. The Hilbert scheme of points on a surface

Let SS be a smooth quasi-projective surface, and set r=1r=1, so that QuotS⁡(L,n)=Hilbn⁡S\Quot_{S}(L,n)=\Hilb^{n}S for every line bundle LL. We know by Formula (2.9) that

𝖹𝒪S​(t)=Exp⁡([S]​∑n>0tn1,n).\mathsf{Z}_{\mathscr{O}_{S}}(t)=\Exp\left([S]\sum_{n>0}{}_{1,n}t^{n}\right).

On the other hand, by Göttsche’s formula [7],

𝖹𝒪S​(t)=Exp⁡([S]​t1−L​t)=Exp⁡([S]​∑n>0Ln−1​tn).\mathsf{Z}_{\mathscr{O}_{S}}(t)=\Exp\left(\frac{[S]t}{1-\mdmathbb{L}t}\right)=\Exp\left([S]\sum_{n>0}\mdmathbb{L}^{n-1}t^{n}\right).

By the injectivity of Exp\Exp, we conclude that on a surface SS one has

(−1,nLn−1)[S]=0.({}_{1,n}-\mdmathbb{L}^{n-1})[S]=0.

However, this relation holds universally for every quasi-projective surface, in particular for S=P2S=\mdmathbb P^{2} and S=A1×P1S=\mdmathbb A^{1}\times\mdmathbb P^{1}. Therefore

(−1,nLn−1)(1+L+L2)=0=(−1,nLn−1)(L+L2),({}_{1,n}-\mdmathbb{L}^{n-1})(1+\mdmathbb{L}+\mdmathbb{L}^{2})=0=({}_{1,n}-\mdmathbb{L}^{n-1})(\mdmathbb{L}+\mdmathbb{L}^{2}),

(3.10) 𝖯1​(t)=∑n≥0[Hilbn⁡(A2)0]​tn=∏n≥1(1−Ln−1​tn)−1.\mathsf{P}_{1}(t)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\,\bigl[\Hilb^{n}(\mdmathbb A^{2})_{0}\bigr]t^{n}=\prod_{n\geq 1}\,\bigl(1-\mdmathbb{L}^{n-1}t^{n}\bigr)^{-1}.

∑n≥0[HilbnA2→�nSymnA2]=Exp∪(∑n>0Ln−1[A2→�nSymnA2])\sum_{n\geq 0}\,\left[\Hilb^{n}\mdmathbb A^{2}\xrightarrow{\sigma_{n}}\Sym^{n}\mdmathbb A^{2}\right]=\Exp_{\cup}\left(\sum_{n>0}\mdmathbb{L}^{n-1}\boxtimes\bigl[\mdmathbb A^{2}\xrightarrow{\Delta_{n}}\Sym^{n}\mdmathbb A^{2}\bigr]\right)

in K0​(VarSym⁡A2)K_{0}(\mathrm{Var}_{\Sym\mdmathbb A^{2}}).

Remark 3.8.

The relation (3.10) was already proved in [8], and it was exploited in [10] to provide a motivic check of the classification of modules of length 33 and 44 over the polynomial ring k⁡[x,y]k[x,y].

4. A motivic-to-geometric open problem

Let CC be a smooth quasi-projective curve. The punctual Quot scheme

Pr,n⊂QuotC⁡(𝒪⊕r,n)P_{r,n}\subset\Quot_{C}(\mathscr{O}^{\oplus r},n)

parameterises quotients 𝒪⊕rQ\mathscr{O}^{\oplus r}\twoheadrightarrow Q entirely supported at a single (fixed) point p∈Cp\in C. As proved in [1, Prop. 2.6], one has

Pr,1=Pr−1.P_{r,1}=\mdmathbb P^{r-1}.

How can one describe Pr,nP_{r,n} for n>1n>1? The relation

𝖯r​(t)=Exp⁡([Pr−1]​t)=�Pr−1​(t)\mathsf{P}_{r}(t)=\Exp\left(\bigl[\mdmathbb P^{r-1}\bigr]t\right)=\zeta_{\mdmathbb P^{r-1}}(t)

established in Equation (3.5) translates into the motivic identity

(4.1) [Pr,n]=[Symn⁡Pr−1]=[Symn⁡Pr,1].\bigl[P_{r,n}\bigr]=\bigl[\Sym^{n}\mdmathbb P^{r-1}\bigr]=\bigl[\Sym^{n}P_{r,1}\bigr].

It thus makes sense to ask the following:

Question 4.1.

What is the geometric meaning of the relation (4.1)? Can one geometrically compare the schemes Pr,nP_{r,n} and Symn⁡Pr,1\Sym^{n}P_{r,1}?
